title: Longest Rising Subsequence
statement:
Given an integer array nums, return the length of its longest strictly increasing subsequence.

A subsequence keeps the original order but may skip elements; it does not have to be contiguous. Strictly increasing means each kept value is larger than the one before it, so equal values cannot both be kept.

examples.why: 4, 5, 6, 7. Taking every next value that is bigger, starting from 4, grabs 10 and gets stuck at length 2.
Equal values do not rise, so only one 3 can be kept.
2, 6, 8. The 1 comes last, so it cannot start a run before them.

hints: For each position, ask: what is the longest rising subsequence that ends exactly here?
It ends with nums[i], and the element before it is some earlier nums[j] < nums[i]. So len(i) = 1 + the largest len(j) over those j. That is O(n²).

Faster: keep tails[k] = the smallest possible last value of a rising subsequence of length k + 1. For each x, binary-search the first tail ≥ x and replace it with x, or append x if none. The answer is tails.length.

explain.intuition:
O(n²) DP. State: len(i) = length of the longest rising subsequence that ends at index i. Recurrence: the value before nums[i] is some earlier, smaller nums[j], so len(i) = 1 + max(len(j) for j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]), or 1 if there is none. The answer is the largest len(i). Fixing the end point is what makes this work: "longest in the first i values" would not tell you which value you can extend.

O(n log n), patience method. Keep an array tails where tails[k] is the smallest last value of any rising subsequence of length k + 1 seen so far. A smaller tail is always better, because it is easier to extend. tails is strictly increasing (a length-3 run ends above some length-2 run), so it can be binary-searched. For each x: find the first tail ≥ x and replace it with x (x makes an equal-length run with a smaller end), or append x if all tails are smaller (x extends the longest run). tails is not itself a valid subsequence: for [2, 6, 8, 1] it ends as [1, 6, 8]. Only its length is the answer.
steps: O(n²): len[i] = 1 + max(len[j]) over j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]; answer = max of len.
O(n log n): start with an empty tails. Meaning: tails[k] = smallest last value of a rising subsequence of length k + 1.
For each x, binary-search the first index k with tails[k] ≥ x (lower bound).
If k equals tails.length, append x; otherwise set tails[k] = x.
pitfalls: Searching for the first tail > x (upper bound). Equal values then extend each other, and [3, 3, 3] returns 3: that counts non-decreasing runs.
Returning tails as the subsequence. It mixes values from different runs; [2, 6, 8, 1] gives [1, 6, 8], which is not in order in the input.
Returning len[n − 1] instead of the maximum. The longest run need not end at the last element, as the third example shows.

solutions.title: Take or skip, recursively
solutions.idea: Walk the array remembering the last kept value; at each element either skip it or keep it if it is larger. Explores every subsequence.

solutions.title: Longest run ending at each index
solutions.idea: len[i] = 1 + the best len[j] over earlier, smaller values. Quadratic, fine for a few thousand elements.

solutions.title: Smallest tail per length, with binary search
solutions.idea: tails[k] is the smallest end of a rising run of length k + 1. Each value replaces the first tail ≥ it, or extends the array.
